# SMTP line-length limits — RFC 5321 (October 2008), §4.5.3.1

## 1. Answer table

| Line type | RFC 5321 section | Max total length | Terminator counted? | Other overhead inside the count |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Text line** (mail data / message content line) | 4.5.3.1.6 | **1000 octets** | Yes, `<CRLF>` (2 octets) is included | Excludes the leading dot duplicated for transparency (dot-stuffing). No other overhead. |
| **Reply line** | 4.5.3.1.5 | **512 octets** | Yes, `<CRLF>` (2 octets) is included | Includes the 3-digit reply code and the separator (`-` for a non-final multiline line, `SP` for the final line). |
| **Command line** (given for completeness — the RFC's separate limit, often confused with "text line") | 4.5.3.1.4 | **512 octets** | Yes, `<CRLF>` (2 octets) is included | Includes the command word (verb) and all parameters. |

Unit is **octets**, not characters. The 1000-octet text-line figure is the number the request names as "SMTP text line"; the 512-octet reply-line figure is the second number requested.

## 2. Normative text (verbatim, RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1)

> **4.5.3.1.4. Command Line**
> The maximum total length of a command line including the command word and the <CRLF> is 512 octets. SMTP extensions may be used to increase this limit.
>
> **4.5.3.1.5. Reply Line**
> The maximum total length of a reply line including the reply code and the <CRLF> is 512 octets. More information may be conveyed through multiple-line replies.
>
> **4.5.3.1.6. Text Line**
> The maximum total length of a text line including the <CRLF> is 1000 octets (not counting the leading dot duplicated for transparency). This number may be increased by the use of SMTP Service Extensions.
>
> **4.5.3.1.7. Message Content**
> The maximum total length of a message content (including any message header section as well as the message body) MUST BE at least 64K octets.

Adjacent limits in the same subsection, for context and for cross-checking implementations: local-part ≤ 64 octets (4.5.3.1.1), domain ≤ 255 octets (4.5.3.1.2), path ≤ 256 octets including punctuation and element separators (4.5.3.1.3), recipient buffer ≥ 100 recipients (4.5.3.1.8).

These are **minimum maximums**: they bound what a conforming sender may emit and set a floor on what every receiver MUST be able to accept. A server may accept longer lines; it MUST accept at least these.

## 3. What the counts include — exact octet budgets

### 3.1 Reply line — 512 octets total

Grammar (RFC 5321 §4.1.2 / §4.2.1):

```
Reply-line = *( Reply-code "-" [ textstring ] CRLF )
             Reply-code [ SP textstring ] CRLF
Reply-code = %x32-35 %x30-35 %x30-39      ; three digits, first 2-5, then 0-5, then 0-9
textstring = 1*( %d09 / %d32-126 )        ; HT, SP, printable US-ASCII
```

Budget for one line (multiline continuation form `250-...CRLF` and final form `250 ...CRLF` are identical in size):

```
  reply code        3 octets
  separator         1 octet   ('-' or SP)
  reply text      ≤ 506 octets
  CRLF              2 octets
  -----------------------------
  total           ≤ 512 octets
```

So the maximum reply *text* is **506 octets** when the separator octet is present. (RFC 5321 §4.1.2 says "The space (blank) following the reply code is considered part of the text" — that is a semantic statement about what the client treats as text; either way the SP sits inside the 512-octet budget, so the budget arithmetic above is unchanged. The SP is optional on the final line and clients MUST tolerate its absence.)

The 512-octet limit is **per line**. A multiline reply may contain any number of lines; there is no aggregate limit in RFC 5321, only "More information may be conveyed through multiple-line replies." Each line, including the last, is independently ≤ 512 octets, and all lines MUST carry the same reply code.

### 3.2 Text line — 1000 octets total

```
  content octets  ≤ 998 octets
  CRLF              2 octets
  -----------------------------
  total           ≤ 1000 octets   (excludes the transparency dot)
```

Transparency rule: a data line whose first octet is `.` is transmitted with one extra leading `.` (dot-stuffing, RFC 5321 §4.5.2). That duplicated dot is **not** counted. Consequence: a receiver must be prepared to read up to **1001 octets** before the terminating CRLF on the wire for a maximum-length dot-stuffed line (998 content + 1 stuffed dot + 2 CRLF), of which only 1000 count against the limit. A zero-length line is legal and occupies exactly 2 octets (the bare CRLF).

### 3.3 Command line — 512 octets total (for completeness)

```
  command text (verb + SP + parameters)  ≤ 510 octets
  CRLF                                      2 octets
  ------------------------------------------------
  total                                  ≤ 512 octets
```

Worked example — a maximum-length `MAIL FROM` command:

```
MAIL FROM:<reverse-path> [SP params]<CRLF>
  "MAIL FROM:<"            11
  reverse-path           ≤ 256   (4.5.3.1.3, includes the angle brackets)
  ... remaining budget for ESMTP parameters: 510 - 11 - 256 = 243 octets
```

This is why a `MAIL FROM`/`RCPT TO` line can never legitimately approach 512 octets from the address alone: the 256-octet path limit binds first.

### 3.4 Sanity check on the three limits

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| 3 + 1 + 506 + 2 = 512 (reply) | ✓ exactly at the limit |
| 510 + 2 = 512 (command) | ✓ exactly at the limit |
| 998 + 2 = 1000 (text) | ✓ exactly at the limit |
| 998 + 1 (transparency dot) + 2 = 1001 wire octets for a max text line | ✓ consistent with "not counting the leading dot" |
| 512 ≤ 1000 | ✓ no conflict: reply/command lines are not "text lines" in the RFC's terminology |

## 4. Common misreadings to avoid

1. **"512 is the text line limit."** No. 512 is command line and reply line. The text line (message content) limit is 1000. Mixing these up is the single most frequent error.
2. **"The limit excludes CRLF."** No — all three limits are stated "including the <CRLF>". A 512-octet buffer that must also hold CRLF is 2 octets short.
3. **"1000 characters."** No — 1000 **octets**. With SMTPUTF8 (RFC 6531) a line can contain multi-octet UTF-8 sequences; the octet count still governs. 1000 octets of UTF-8 may be fewer than 1000 characters.
4. **"The reply limit is for the whole reply."** No — per line; multiline replies extend the total.
5. **"The dot counts."** The transparency dot does not count toward the 1000; the wire line can therefore be 1001 octets.
6. **"RFC 821/2821 numbers."** RFC 5321 obsoletes RFC 821 and RFC 2821; pin citations to RFC 5321 (October 2008). The 512/512/1000 figures are unchanged from RFC 2821, but the citation should be RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.4–.6.

## 5. Implementation guidance

### 5.1 Constants

```python
MAX_COMMAND_LINE = 512    # octets, INCLUDING CRLF
MAX_REPLY_LINE   = 512    # octets, INCLUDING CRLF and reply code, per line
MAX_TEXT_LINE    = 1000   # octets, INCLUDING CRLF, EXCLUDING transparency dot
MAX_TEXT_LINE_WIRE = MAX_TEXT_LINE + 1   # 1001: dot-stuffed worst case
CRLF_LEN = 2
```

### 5.2 Line reader with hard caps (no unbounded buffering)

```python
def read_line(sock, limit_incl_crlf):
    """Read one CRLF-terminated line. Returns (octets_without_crlf, too_long).
    Reads at most limit_incl_crlf octets; never grows the buffer past the cap."""
    buf = bytearray()
    while True:
        b = sock.read(1)
        if not b:
            raise ConnectionError("EOF before CRLF")
        buf += b
        if len(buf) >= 2 and buf[-2:] == b"\r\n":
            return bytes(buf[:-2]), False
        if len(buf) >= limit_incl_crlf:
            # no CRLF yet and we are already at the cap -> line is over-long
            drain_to_crlf(sock)          # consume the rest, bounded by a hard ceiling
            return bytes(buf), True

def drain_to_crlf(sock, ceiling=65536):
    seen = 0
    while seen < ceiling:
        b = sock.read(1)
        if not b or b == b"\n":
            return
        seen += 1
```

Call sites:

- **Command lines:** `read_line(conn, 512)`. On `too_long`, reply `500 Line too long` (RFC 5321 §4.2.3 lists 500 as syntax error / command line too long; 500 is the conventional choice) and keep the session alive unless the client keeps offending.
- **Reply lines (client side):** `read_line(conn, 512)` per line. Reject/abort on over-long rather than accepting silently; the client's only obligation is to be able to *receive* 512-octet lines.
- **DATA lines:** `read_line(conn, 1001)` — the extra octet covers the transparency dot; after reading, un-stuff (drop one leading `.` when the line starts with `.`) and then assert the un-stuffed line ≤ 1000 octets including CRLF. A lone `.` line terminates the data.

### 5.3 Error handling notes

- RFC 5321 does not assign a dedicated reply code for an over-long **DATA** line. Practical choices: accept and truncate (lossy — avoid), accept and store (exceeds the minimum but is legal for a server to do), or reject the message after DATA with a 5xx (e.g. `552` or `554`) and log. Whatever is chosen, do not let a long line desynchronize the parser.
- On the **client** side, treat a >512-octet reply line as a protocol violation but do not hang: cap reads, then abandon the reply and report the error to the caller.
- Never derive buffer sizes from the *content* length (`SIZE`, RFC 1870); line length and message length are independent limits.

### 5.4 Extension interactions (out of scope for the base answer, listed so nobody mis-cites them)

- 4.5.3.1.4 and 4.5.3.1.6 both say the limit "may be increased by the use of SMTP Service Extensions". The base numbers above are what a peer may assume **without** a negotiated extension.
- The LIMITS extension (`draft-freed-smtp-limits`, referenced in the emailcore working-group discussion of §4.5.3) is the proposed mechanism for advertising larger limits; it is not part of RFC 5321.
- CHUNKING/BDAT (RFC 3030) removes the CRLF-and-dot framing for message content entirely, so the 1000-octet text-line limit does not apply to BDAT payload framing — but it is a separate negotiated extension.
- RFC 1870 SIZE limits total message size, not line length. It does not change 512 or 1000.

## 6. One-paragraph answer (ready to paste)

Under RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1, the maximum total length of a **text line** (a line of mail data) is **1000 octets including the terminating CRLF** and **not counting the leading dot duplicated for transparency** — i.e. 998 octets of content plus 2 octets of CRLF, with a dot-stuffed maximum-length line occupying 1001 octets on the wire. The maximum total length of a **reply line** is **512 octets including the 3-digit reply code, the one-octet separator (`-` or SP), the reply text, and the terminating CRLF** — i.e. at most 506 octets of reply text; the limit applies per line, and a multiline reply may carry any number of such lines. (For comparison, §4.5.3.1.4 limits a **command line** to 512 octets including the command word, its parameters, and the CRLF.) All three figures are octet counts, all three include the CRLF terminator, and all three may be raised by negotiated SMTP service extensions.

# Hours of service, property-carrying CMV — 49 CFR § 395.3(a)

## 1. Answers

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Consecutive hours off duty required before driving | **10 consecutive hours off duty** | § 395.3(a)(1) |
| 2 | Consecutive hours on duty after which the driver may no longer drive | **14 consecutive hours** (measured from coming on duty) | § 395.3(a)(2) |
| 3 | Total hours that may be driven within that period | **11 hours** | § 395.3(a)(3)(i) |

These are the standard limits for a driver of a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle in interstate commerce, assuming no exception in § 395.1 applies.

## 2. Governing text (verbatim)

> § 395.3 Maximum driving time for property-carrying vehicles.
>
> (a) Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1, no motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, unless the driver complies with the following requirements:
>
> (1) **Start of work shift.** A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty;
>
> (2) **14-hour period.** A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty.
>
> (3) **Driving time and interruptions of driving periods** —
>
> (i) **Driving time.** A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.
>
> (ii) **Interruption of driving time.** Except for drivers who qualify for either of the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least a consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. A consecutive 30-minute interruption of driving status may be satisfied either by off-duty, sleeper berth or on-duty not driving time or by a combination of off-duty, sleeper berth and on-duty not driving time.

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/chapter-III/subchapter-B/part-395/section-395.3 ; corroborated by https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title49-vol5/pdf/CFR-2025-title49-vol5-sec395-3.pdf and https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/395.3 . Citation history: 76 FR 81188 (Dec. 27, 2011), as amended at 78 FR 58485, 78 FR 64181, 84 FR 48081, 85 FR 33452.

## 3. How the three numbers interlock

The three figures are three separate constraints that apply simultaneously, not three ways of stating one limit.

- **10 hours off duty** is a *reset*. It is a minimum continuous block that must precede any driving.
- **14 hours** is a *window*. It begins when the driver comes on duty after a qualifying 10-hour (or greater) off-duty period, and it runs on the clock. It is **elapsed time**, not accumulated on-duty time: a 2-hour off-duty lunch inside the shift does not buy the driver a 16-hour day.
- **11 hours** is a *cap on driving* inside that 14-hour window. The remaining 3 hours of the 14 can be used for non-driving on-duty work (loading, fueling, inspections, paperwork), or not used at all.

So the maximum shape of a legal shift is: 10+ consecutive hours off duty → come on duty → up to 14 consecutive hours of combined driving and on-duty-not-driving, of which no more than 11 hours may be driving → then at least 10 consecutive hours off duty before any further driving.

### Worked example (values checked against every limit above)

- 20:00 (prior day) — driver goes off duty.
- 06:00 — driver comes on duty. 10 consecutive hours off duty satisfied; the 14-hour window opens and will close at **20:00**.
- 06:00–08:00 — driving (2.0 h; running total 2.0 h).
- 08:00–09:00 — on-duty not driving (1.0 h of the 3 available).
- 09:00–12:00 — driving (3.0 h; running total 5.0 h).
- 12:00–12:30 — 30-minute interruption, off duty. This satisfies § 395.3(a)(3)(ii); it does **not** stop or extend the 14-hour clock.
- 12:30–16:30 — driving (4.0 h; running total 9.0 h).
- 16:30–17:00 — on-duty not driving (0.5 h; total non-driving on duty 1.5 h).
- 17:00–19:00 — driving (2.0 h; running total 11.0 h — the cap, reached exactly).
- 19:00–20:00 — on-duty not driving (1.0 h; total non-driving on duty 2.5 h).
- **20:00 — the 14th hour. No further driving is permitted**, even though only 2.5 of the 3 non-driving hours have been used and the driver could still perform non-driving work. Driving may resume only after 10 consecutive hours off duty (i.e., not before 06:00 the next day).

Check: driving 11.0 h ≤ 11 h cap ✔; window 14.0 h = 14 h limit ✔; driving 11.0 h ≤ 14 h window ✔; non-driving on duty 2.5 h ≤ 3 h residual ✔; no driving after hour 14 ✔; 30-minute interruption taken before more than 8 hours of driving accumulated without one ✔ (interruption at 5.0 cumulative driving hours).

## 4. Precision points that change how the numbers are applied

1. **The 14-hour limit is a limit on *driving*, not on all work.** § 395.3(a)(2) says the driver "may not drive" after the 14th hour. Non-driving on-duty work after hour 14 is not prohibited by (a)(2), but it counts toward the 60/70-hour limits in § 395.3(b), and the driver still cannot drive again until a fresh 10 consecutive hours off duty.
2. **"On duty" for the 14-hour window means elapsed time since coming on duty**, not the sum of on-duty log lines. The regulation's phrase is "a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty." The question's framing ("after how many consecutive hours on duty") describes the same threshold; the value is 14 hours either way, but the distinction matters for anyone applying it to a log.
3. **Short off-duty breaks do not extend the window.** Only a full 10-consecutive-hour (or longer) off-duty period restarts the 14 hours. Drivers using the split sleeper-berth provision in § 395.1(g) may exclude a qualifying sleeper-berth period from the calculation; that mechanism is outside the three figures asked and is not quantified here.
4. **The 30-minute interruption is a fourth, independent constraint** under § 395.3(a)(3)(ii). It applies to any driver who does not qualify for the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2). It is satisfied by off-duty, sleeper berth, or on-duty-not-driving time, or a combination, and it does not extend the 14-hour window.
5. **Weekly caps are separate.** § 395.3(b) independently bars driving after 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days (carrier does not operate every day) or 70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days (carrier operates every day). § 395.3(c) allows any such 7- or 8-day period to end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours (the "34-hour restart"). These bound total weekly driving; they are not the answer to ask 3, which is the within-shift cap.
6. **Passenger-carrying vehicles are different.** § 395.5 sets 10 hours of driving following 8 consecutive hours off duty and a 15-hour on-duty window. The figures above do not apply to passenger-carrying CMVs.

## 5. Scope, assumptions, and what would change the answer

- **Assumed:** the driver operates a property-carrying CMV in interstate commerce, so Part 395 applies as written; the driver is not operating in Alaska; no exemption or exception applies; the question asks for the standard limits, not a compliance determination on a specific record of duty status.
- **§ 395.3(a) opens with "Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1."** Relief provisions that can alter these figures include the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e), the Alaska provisions in § 395.1(h) (which for property-carrying vehicles substitute 15 hours of driving following 10 consecutive hours off duty, a 20-hour on-duty limit, and 70/80-hour weekly limits), and the adverse-driving-conditions exception in § 395.1(b). The text of the general adverse-conditions exception was not among the sources retrieved for this answer, so no extended figure is stated here; if that exception is in scope, the governing text of § 395.1(b) should be consulted before relying on the 11- and 14-hour numbers for a specific run.
- **If the driver is not in interstate commerce**, state intrastate hours-of-service rules may differ and this answer would not control.

## 6. One-line restatement

A property-carrying CMV driver must take **10 consecutive hours off duty** before driving, may not drive after **14 consecutive hours** have elapsed since coming on duty, and may drive no more than **11 hours** within that 14-hour period — plus a 30-minute interruption of driving status before more than 8 hours of driving accumulate without one.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2025-title49-vol5/pdf/cfr-2025-title49-vol5-sec395-3.pdf and 15 on ecfr.gov/current/title-49/part-395. The first reads: "(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty;"

# Rescission Timing Determination — 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i)

**Basis:** Current text of 12 CFR § 1026.23 (eCFR, current; GovInfo CFR 2025 title 12 vol. 9; CFPB Regulation Z page and its 2026-04-08 and 2023-04-19 snapshots — text identical across all five retrievals), plus Official Interpretation, Supp. I, comment 23(a)(3)-1. Scope is limited to the timing rules of § 1026.23(a)(3)(i); procedures and effects of rescission (§ 1026.23(a)(2), (b), (c), (d)) are referenced only where they define the trigger.

## 1. Until when a consumer may exercise the right to rescind (general rule)

**Rule (quoted):** "The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last."

**Answer: 3 business days.** The period runs from whichever of the three triggering events occurs **last** — not from consummation alone:

| Trigger | Notes |
|---|---|
| Consummation | The transaction is consummated (§ 1026.2(a)(13)). |
| Delivery of the § 1026.23(b) notice | Must be the appendix H model form or a "substantially similar notice" (§ 1026.23(b)(2)). A defective notice is treated as non-delivery. |
| Delivery of all material disclosures | All of them; partial delivery does not start the clock. |

**Deadline mechanics.** The deadline is **midnight at the end of the third business day** after the last trigger. "Business day" for rescission purposes is a day on which the creditor's offices are open to the public for carrying on substantially all of its business functions (§ 1026.2(a)(6)); Saturdays, Sundays and federal holidays count only if the creditor is in fact open.

**Exercise is effective on dispatch, not receipt.** Under § 1026.23(a)(2), notice is given when mailed, when filed for telegraphic transmission, or, if sent by other means, when delivered to the creditor's designated place of business. The consumer must dispatch within the period; the creditor need not receive it within the period.

**Worked example (Supp. I, comment 23(a)(3)-1.ii.B).** Disclosures and consummation Friday, June 1; rescission notice delivered Monday, June 4 → period expires midnight Thursday, June 7 (June 4 is the last trigger; the three following business days are June 5, 6, 7).

## 2. When the right expires if the notice or material disclosures are never delivered

**Rule (quoted):** "If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first."

**Answer: 3 years after consummation**, but subject to two earlier cutoff events that run in the creditor's favor:

1. **Three years after consummation** — measured from consummation, not from any later event, and not reset by later delivery.
2. **Transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property** — cuts the period short even inside three years.
3. **Sale of the property** — cuts the period short even inside three years.

Whichever of the three occurs **first** governs. Only one mechanism lengthens the period: "In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act" (15 U.S.C. 1635(f)) — where an enforcing agency commences a proceeding within the three-year window and obtains a finding of violation on a matter on which the rescission right is based, the period extends (statutorily, one year past the expiration date). No other extension exists.

**Critical distinction — "never delivered" vs. "delivered late."**

- **Never delivered** (neither the § 1026.23(b) notice nor all material disclosures ever delivered) → three-year tail applies, ending at the earliest of the three events above.
- **Delivered late** (delivered after consummation but before the three-year mark) → there is no three-year tail. The ordinary rule of § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) applies and the consumer has three business days from the later delivery. Supp. I, comment 23(b)(1)-4: if the notice is given May 15 but disclosures were given and the transaction consummated May 10, the three-business-day period runs from May 15.
- **Partially delivered** (some but not all material disclosures) → treated as material disclosures not delivered → three-year tail.

## 3. Operative definitions

**Material disclosures** (§ 1026.23(a)(3)(ii)) — the required disclosures of: the annual percentage rate; the finance charge; the amount financed; the total of payments; the payment schedule; and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g). Nothing else qualifies; a disclosure outside this list that is missing does not trigger the three-year tail.

**Required notice** (§ 1026.23(b)(1)–(2)) — must state the retention/acquisition of the security interest in the principal dwelling, the consumer's right to rescind, how to exercise it with a form designating the creditor's business address, the effects of rescission under (d), and the date the rescission period expires; and must be the appendix H model form or substantially similar.

## 4. Computation procedure

1. Fix the consummation date.
2. Determine whether the § 1026.23(b) notice was delivered in proper form, and whether **all** material disclosures were delivered. Record delivery dates and the delivery method (mail, electronic per E-SIGN consent, in person).
3. If all three events occurred: last event date → count three business days (creditor's open days) → deadline is **midnight** of the third business day.
4. If notice or any material disclosure was never delivered: expiration = **earlier of** (a) the third anniversary of consummation, (b) transfer of all of the consumer's interest, (c) sale of the property.
5. If an enforcing agency proceeding is pending within the window, apply the § 125(f) extension before fixing the expiration date.
6. Convention for the three-year date: the regulation fixes no time of day. Record the expiration as the calendar date three years after consummation and treat any written notice dispatched on or before that date as timely — a creditor-conservative convention that avoids a timeliness dispute at the margin.

**Example:** consummation 2024-03-15 with no notice and no material disclosures ever delivered → right expires 2027-03-15, unless all of the consumer's interest is transferred or the property is sold before then, in which case it expires on that earlier date.

## 5. Adjacent cases that change the answer

- **Added security interest** (§ 1026.23(a)(1)): adding a security interest in the principal dwelling to an existing obligation is itself a transaction, but rescission reaches only the added security interest. No new material disclosures are required; **delivery of the required notice begins the rescission period**. If that notice is never delivered, the three-year tail applies to the added interest.
- **Exempt transactions** (§ 1026.23(f), e.g., residential mortgage transactions, and § 1026.23(a)(1) carve-outs): no right of rescission exists, so neither timing rule is reached. Confirm exemption status before applying either answer.
- **Open-end credit**: governed by § 1026.15, not § 1026.23; do not apply these periods to a HELOC without checking § 1026.15(a)(3).

## 6. Compliance controls

- Retain evidence of delivery of the notice and of each material disclosure for **at least three years plus the record-retention period**, not merely the two years required by § 1026.25 — the rescission exposure outlives the retention floor.
- Log the last-trigger date and the computed deadline in the origination file; the § 1026.23(b)(1)(v) notice must state the expiration date, so the computation is a disclosure input, not just a servicing note.
- Flag any file where the notice form departs from appendix H, or where a material disclosure was corrected post-consummation: a non-compliant notice is functionally non-delivery and converts a three-business-day exposure into a three-year one.

## 7. Authorities

12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(1), (a)(2), (a)(3)(i), (a)(3)(ii), (b)(1), (b)(2), (f); § 1026.2(a)(6), (a)(13); § 1026.25; Supp. I, comments 23(a)(3)-1 and 23(b)(1)-4; 15 U.S.C. 1635(f). Note as outside the regulation text: *Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans, Inc.*, 574 U.S. 259 (2015) — the right is exercised by written notice dispatched within the period; suit need not be filed within it. Confirm current case law with counsel before relying on it in a dispute.

ANNUAL OCCUPATIONAL DOSE LIMITS FOR ADULT RADIATION WORKERS — 10 CFR § 20.1201(a)

Governing text (verbatim, current eCFR / GovInfo 2024–2025 text):
"(a) The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.
(1) An annual limit, which is the more limiting of—
(i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or
(ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).
(2) The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are:
(i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and
(ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity."

1. TOTAL EFFECTIVE DOSE EQUIVALENT (TEDE)
   Limit: 5 rems per year = 0.05 Sv per year (50 mSv/y).
   Citation: § 20.1201(a)(1)(i).
   Note on structure: § 20.1201(a)(1) sets the annual limit as "the more limiting of" (i) TEDE = 5 rems or (ii) deep-dose equivalent plus committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens = 50 rems (0.5 Sv). The 5 rem TEDE value is the headline effective-dose limit; the 50 rem organ figure in (a)(1)(ii) is a separate, non-binding-unless-limiting constraint and is not a substitute for the 5 rem TEDE limit.

2. LENS OF THE EYE
   Limit: lens dose equivalent of 15 rems per year = 0.15 Sv per year (150 mSv/y).
   Citation: § 20.1201(a)(2)(i).
   Note: 15 rems is the value in the current text. The source note to § 20.1201 lists amendment at 72 FR 68059 (Dec. 4, 2007); the pre-2007 lens figure (3 rems) is superseded and must not be used.

3. SKIN OF THE WHOLE BODY
   Limit: shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rems per year = 0.5 Sv per year (500 mSv/y), applicable to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity.
   Citation: § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii).
   Note on how the quantity is assigned: under § 20.1201(c), the assigned shallow-dose equivalent is the dose averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure.

4. UNIT CONVERSION
   Conventional ratio used by the regulation: 1 rem = 0.01 Sv (1 Sv = 100 rem).
   5 rem  × 0.01 = 0.05 Sv
   15 rem × 0.01 = 0.15 Sv
   50 rem × 0.01 = 0.5 Sv
   These computed values match the sievert figures printed parenthetically in the regulation itself.

SUMMARY TABLE
   Quantity                          rems/y    sieverts/y   Citation
   Total effective dose equivalent   5         0.05         § 20.1201(a)(1)(i)
   Lens of the eye (lens dose equiv.)15        0.15         § 20.1201(a)(2)(i)
   Skin of whole body (shallow-dose) 50        0.5          § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii)

SCOPE BOUNDARIES (not part of the three requested values, stated to prevent misapplication):
- Minors: 10% of the adult limits, i.e. 0.5 rem (0.005 Sv) TEDE, 1.5 rem (0.015 Sv) lens, 5 rem (0.05 Sv) skin — § 20.1207. Different limit; not the adult answer.
- Declared pregnancy / embryo-fetus: 0.5 rem (0.005 Sv) to the embryo/fetus during the entire gestation period — § 20.1208. Not applicable to the adult worker's own occupational limit.
- Planned special exposures: governed by § 20.1206 (in any year, the numerical values of § 20.1201(a); over a lifetime, five times those values). Excluded from the (a) limits by the opening words of (a).
- Extremities: share the 50 rem (0.5 Sv) shallow-dose equivalent limit with whole-body skin — § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii).
- Lens values in NRC guidance or ICRP recommendations outside the regulation (e.g., a 20 mSv/y averaged lens criterion) are not the § 20.1201(a) limit and are not reported here.

SOURCE VERIFICATION: values confirmed against the current eCFR text at ecfr.gov/current/title-10/section-20.1201 and the GovInfo CFR-2024-title10-vol1 and CFR-2025-title10-vol1 compilations of § 20.1201; all fetches agree word-for-word on the three figures above. Verify against the latest eCFR text at time of use, since dose limits have been amended historically (1991 promulgation; amendments at 60 FR 20185, 63 FR 39482, 67 FR 16304, 72 FR 68059).

question: P8
answer:
# Fall Protection Trigger and Permitted Systems — 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1)

**Prepared by:** Safety Engineer  
**Subject:** Height at which fall protection is required on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge, and the systems that satisfy the requirement  
**Basis:** 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), Subpart M (Fall Protection), Construction Safety and Health Regulations, as currently published in the e-CFR and as printed in CFR 2025 Title 29, Vol. 8. Subpart M final rule published 9 August 1994 (59 FR 40730), effective 6 February 1995; the 6-foot trigger in (b)(1) has been unchanged since that rule.

---

## 1. Answers

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Height above a lower level at which protection is required | **6 feet (1.8 m) or more** |
| 2 | Systems that satisfy the requirement | **Guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems** (any one of the three; employer's choice) |

---

## 2. Controlling regulatory text

29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1) — *Unprotected sides and edges*:

> "Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems."

Three operative elements, read in order:

1. **Scope of employee exposure** — an employee must be *on a walking/working surface*. The parenthetical "(horizontal and vertical surface)" is deliberate: vertical surfaces (formwork faces, walls, structural steel faces used as work platforms) count. It is not limited to floors and decks.
2. **The trigger** — the surface has an *unprotected side or edge* that is **6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level**. The relative clause modifies the side/edge (i.e., the elevation drop at the edge), not the employee's body position; the measurement is the vertical distance from the walking/working surface down to the lower level.
3. **The required remedy** — protection "by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems."

### Note on the two figures
"6 feet (1.8 m)" is a soft metric conversion. 6 ft = 1.8288 m, rounded in the regulation to 1.8 m. The operative federal dimension is **6 feet**; 1.8 m is the published approximate equivalent and should not be read as an independent, slightly lower trigger.

### Boundary behavior
- **At exactly 6 ft 0 in** — the requirement **applies**. The text is "6 feet (1.8 m) **or more**," so the boundary is inclusive. Do not treat 6 ft as a safe harbor.
- **Below 6 ft** — (b)(1) does not itself require fall protection. This is **not** a blanket exemption from Subpart M; see § 6 below.

---

## 3. The three permitted systems under (b)(1)

The list is **disjunctive** ("or"). The employer selects **one** system; the standard does not rank them, does not require the "best" system, and does not require more than one. Whatever is selected must be designed, installed, and used to meet the corresponding criteria in **§ 1926.502**:

| System | Governing criteria | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Guardrail system** | § 1926.502(b) | Passive barrier at the edge; prevents the fall |
| **Safety net system** | § 1926.502(c) | Passive; arrests the fall after it occurs |
| **Personal fall arrest system (PFAS)** | § 1926.502(d) | Active; body harness + connecting means + anchorage; arrests the fall |

### 3.1 Guardrail systems — § 1926.502(b) (key criteria)
- Top edge height of top rails (or equivalent member) **42 inches (1.1 m) ± 3 inches (8 cm)** above the walking/working level.
- Midrail **21 inches (53 cm)** above the walking/working level (or equivalent protection such as screening/panels per § 1926.502(b)(4)–(5)).
- Must withstand, without failure, a force of at least **200 lb (890 N)** applied within 2 inches (5.1 cm) of the top edge, in any outward or downward direction.
- Where guardrails are used at hoisting areas, holes, or as the edge barrier for a roof, additional provisions in 502(b) apply (gates, swing gates, etc.).

### 3.2 Safety net systems — § 1926.502(c) (key criteria)
- Installed as close as practicable under the walking/working surface, **but never more than 30 feet (9.1 m) below** that level.
- Must extend outward from the outermost projection of the work surface by a distance keyed to the vertical fall distance (8 ft / 10 ft / 13 ft tiers in 502(c)(2)).
- Mesh openings, perimeter, and drop-test requirements per 502(c)(3)–(7).

### 3.3 Personal fall arrest systems — § 1926.502(d) (key criteria)
- **Body belts are not acceptable** as part of a PFAS (502(d)(1)); a full body harness is required.
- Must limit the **maximum free-fall distance to 6 feet (1.8 m)** (502(d)(16)(ii)) and bring the employee to a complete stop with a **maximum deceleration distance of 3.5 feet (1.07 m)** (502(d)(16)(iv)).
- Anchorage must support at least 5,000 lb per employee attached, or be designed/engineered as part of a complete PFAS with a safety factor of at least two (502(d)(15)).
- Prompt rescue of an employee following a fall is required (502(d)(20)).
- Note: the **6-foot free-fall limit in 502(d)(16)(ii) is a system-design limit, not a fall-protection trigger.** It happens to equal the (b)(1) trigger height; the two numbers serve different functions and must not be conflated.

> **Sourcing caveat.** The dimensional criteria in § 3.1–3.3 come from § 1926.502, which was not part of the retrieved source set (only § 1926.501 was fetched). They are stated here as cross-references for the engineer applying the standard and **should be confirmed against the current § 1926.502 text** before being quoted in a citation-bearing document (e.g., a citation response or a written program). The (b)(1) threshold and system list in § 2 are taken verbatim from the fetched e-CFR / CFR 2025 text and are not in doubt.

---

## 4. How the requirement is applied in the field

1. **Identify the walking/working surface** the employee will occupy — including vertical surfaces (formwork, wall faces).
2. **Identify the unprotected side or edge** — any edge not already guarded by a compliant barrier, cover, or equivalent.
3. **Measure the vertical drop** from that surface, at that edge, to the lower level. Use the lowest level a person could realistically reach, not the nearest incidental obstruction.
4. **Compare to 6 ft 0 in.** If the drop is **6 ft or more**, protection is required. At exactly 6 ft, protection is required.
5. **Select one of the three systems** — guardrail, safety net, or PFAS — and verify it meets § 1926.502 criteria for that system.
6. **Document** the selection and the basis (drawing, fall protection plan, or work procedure) for the specific edge.

---

## 5. What (b)(1) does not permit, and what it does

- **Not permitted by (b)(1) itself:** warning lines, safety monitoring systems, controlled access zones, or a fall protection plan in lieu of a system. Those are available only where another paragraph of § 1926.501 authorizes them (see § 6).
- **Permitted:** the employer may freely choose among guardrail, safety net, and PFAS. Cost or convenience is a legitimate basis for choosing among the three; infeasibility is **not** a defense to providing *none* of them under (b)(1) (contrast the leading-edge exception in (b)(2)(i)).
- The employer may use a combination (e.g., guardrail on one elevation, PFAS on another) so long as each exposed edge is covered by at least one compliant system.

---

## 6. Adjacent provisions that change the answer for specific conditions

The 6-ft trigger is the general rule for unprotected sides and edges, but **it is not the only trigger in Subpart M, and it is not the only list of permitted systems.** If the exposure matches one of the following, the specific paragraph governs:

| Condition | Citation | Trigger | Permitted systems (as stated) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Leading edge construction | (b)(2)(i) | 6 ft or more | Guardrail, safety net, or PFAS; **exception** — where infeasible or a greater hazard, a written fall protection plan per § 1926.502(k) (presumption of feasibility; employer bears the burden) |
| Holes (incl. skylights) | (b)(4) | More than 6 ft | PFAS, **covers**, or guardrails around the hole |
| Formwork / reinforcing steel | (b)(5) | 6 ft or more | PFAS, safety net, or **positioning device system** |
| Ramps, runways, walkways | (b)(6) | 6 ft or more | **Guardrail systems only** |
| Excavations — wells, pits, shafts | (b)(7)(ii) | 6 ft or more in depth | Guardrail, **fences, barricades, or covers** |
| Dangerous equipment | (b)(8)(i) | **Less than 6 ft** | Guardrail or **equipment guards** |
| Dangerous equipment | (b)(8)(ii) | 6 ft or more | Guardrail, PFAS, or safety net |
| Overhand bricklaying | (b)(9)(i) | 6 ft or more | Guardrail, safety net, PFAS, **or controlled access zone** |
| Low-slope roofing | (b)(10) | 6 ft or more | Guardrail, safety net, PFAS, **or a combination of warning line + guardrail/safety net/PFAS/safety monitoring** |
| Steep roofs | (b)(11) | Any width > 6 ft, regardless of height | Guardrail, safety net, or PFAS |
| Wall openings | (b)(14) | Outer bottom edge 6 ft or more above lower level, inner bottom edge < 39 in above surface | Guardrail, safety net, or PFAS |
| Surfaces not otherwise addressed | (b)(15) | 6 ft or more | Guardrail, safety net, or PFAS (subject to § 1926.500(a)(2) scope carve-outs) |

**Key point for the requester:** the answer to "which systems" under **(b)(1) specifically** is the three-system list. Broader lists (covers, warning lines, safety monitoring, controlled access zones, positioning devices, fences, barricades) belong to *other* paragraphs of § 1926.501 and cannot be substituted for the (b)(1) list unless the exposure actually falls under that other paragraph.

---

## 7. Scope and jurisdictional caveats

- **Vertical scope.** § 1926.501 is a **construction** standard (29 CFR Part 1926, Subpart M). For general industry, the analogous walking-working surfaces rule is § 1910.28/1910.29, which uses a **4-foot** trigger for general industry surfaces (and different rules for specific equipment). Do not import the 6-ft construction figure into a general-industry program, or vice versa.
- **Horizontal scope.** This memo answers the **federal** standard. Roughly half the states and two territories operate OSHA-approved State Plans, which must be **at least as effective as** the federal rule but may differ in specifics. Some State Plans use a different construction trigger height — for example, California's construction fall protection requirement is commonly cited at **7.5 ft** rather than 6 ft. **Confirm the applicable State Plan before applying the 6-ft figure to a project in a State Plan jurisdiction.**
- **Scope carve-outs.** § 1926.500(a)(2) removes certain activities from Subpart M coverage entirely (e.g., specified pre-construction inspection/assessment work, certain utility line work, and other enumerated activities). If a carve-out applies, neither (b)(1) nor any other paragraph of § 1926.501 governs. Verify § 1926.500(a)(2) against the specific task.
- **Currency.** Text verified against the e-CFR and CFR 2025 edition. Regulations are amended; re-verify against the e-CFR at the time of use.

---

## 8. One-paragraph answer for direct use

Under 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal or vertical) with an unprotected side or edge that is **6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level** must be protected from falling. Protection must be provided by the use of **guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems** — the employer may choose any one of the three, and the chosen system must meet the applicable criteria of § 1926.502 (guardrails at 502(b), safety nets at 502(c), personal fall arrest at 502(d)). The threshold is inclusive: at exactly 6 feet, protection is required. Where the exposure is a leading edge, hole, ramp, excavation, bricklaying operation, or roofing work, the more specific paragraph of § 1926.501(b)(2)–(15) governs and may permit additional or different means (e.g., covers, warning lines, controlled access zones, or a § 1926.502(k) fall protection plan).

answer:
# Working Time Regulations 1998 (UK) — reg 4(1): the 48-hour average and how a worker is taken outside it

*Scope assumed (state if wrong): adult workers; Great Britain (the WTR 1998 extend to England and Wales and Scotland, 'E+W+S'); the Regulations as amended and in force at the 2025-04-01 version consulted. Northern Ireland has a parallel instrument (SR 1998/386) in materially identical terms. This is a statement of the statutory position, not advice on enforcement or on any individual's contract.*

## 1. The limit (ask 1)

**48 hours per week on average — i.e. an average of 48 hours for each seven days — counting overtime.**

Regulation 4(1), as amended (current text):

> "**Maximum weekly working time** E+W+S
> 4.—(1) [Unless his employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work], a worker's working time, **including overtime**, in any reference period which is applicable in his case shall not exceed an **average of 48 hours for each seven days**."

The as-made text expresses the same limit differently — "Subject to regulation 5, a worker's working time, including overtime, in any reference period which is applicable in his case, shall not exceed 48 hours for each seven days" — and the 1998 original is in the same terms. The figure has never changed: **48**.

Points that fall out of the wording:

1. **It is an average, not a weekly cap.** A single week above 48 hours is not, by itself, a breach; the average over the reference period must not exceed 48. (This is why the answer to ask 2 matters — a worker can lawfully be *rostered* above 48 in a given week even without an opt-out, provided the average holds. The opt-out is what removes the average.)
2. **Overtime is included** — all hours of working time, contractual or voluntary, plus time during which the worker is working, at the employer's disposal and carrying out duties (reg 2(1)).
3. **The default reference period is 17 weeks** (reg 4(3)):
   - reg 4(3)(a): where a relevant agreement applies reg 4 to *successive periods of 17 weeks*, each such period;
   - reg 4(3)(b): otherwise, **any period of 17 weeks** in the course of the worker's employment. Note the significance of "any": absent a relevant agreement fixing successive periods, enforcement (and the worker) may look at *any* rolling 17-week window, not only windows the employer has chosen.
4. **Short service:** where the worker has been employed for less than 17 weeks, the reference period is the period elapsed since the worker started work (reg 4(4)).
5. **Reference period may be varied** by a relevant agreement under reg 23(b) (reg 4(3) is expressly "subject to paragraphs (4) and (5) and any agreement under regulation 23(b)"), and reg 4(5) provides for longer periods in specified cases. Extending the window does not change the 48-hour *rate*; it changes the arithmetic ceiling: the ceiling is always **48 x (number of weeks in the applicable reference period)**. Illustratively: 17 weeks -> 816 hours; 26 weeks -> 1,248 hours. The 48 figure is invariant.
6. **Holiday and other excluded days are neutralised, not counted as zero.** Reg 4(6)-(7): average = (A + B) / C where A = hours of working time in the reference period, B = hours worked in the period immediately after it until the number of days worked equals the number of *excluded days* in the reference period, C = number of weeks in the reference period. "Excluded days" are days of reg 13/13A/15B annual leave, sick leave, maternity/paternity/adoption/parental leave, and days on which the reg 4(1) limit did not apply because the employer had obtained the reg 5 agreement.

**Worked check (compliance arithmetic).** 17-week reference period; worker took 10 days' annual leave (excluded days); A = 730 hours; over the following days on which the worker worked, up to 10 working days, B = 80 hours; C = 17.

> Average = (730 + 80) / 17 = 810 / 17 = **47.65 hours** — within the limit (total 810 <= 816).

Contrast, same facts with A = 740: (740 + 80) / 17 = 820 / 17 = **48.24 hours** — a breach, notwithstanding the small margin. The pass/fail test is always A + B <= 48 x C.

## 2. How a worker is taken outside the limit (ask 2)

**The step: the employer must first obtain the worker's own agreement, in writing, that the reg 4(1) limit shall not apply in the worker's case — the reg 5 "opt-out".**

Regulation 5 (as made; the substance is unchanged, but see the currency note at §5):

> "**Agreement to exclude the maximum**
> 5.—(1) The limit specified in regulation 4(1) shall not apply in relation to a worker who has agreed with his employer in writing that it should not apply in his case, provided that the employer complies with the requirements of paragraph (4).
> (2) An agreement for the purposes of paragraph (1)— (a) may either relate to a specified period or apply indefinitely; and (b) subject to any provision in the agreement for a different period of notice, shall be terminable by the worker by giving not less than seven days' notice to his employer in writing.
> (3) Where an agreement for the purposes of paragraph (1) makes provision for the termination of the agreement after a period of notice, the notice period provided for shall not exceed three months."

### 2.1 Conditions for a valid opt-out (checklist)

| # | Condition | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **In writing** — a signed written agreement (individual); an oral agreement or a mere practice will not do | reg 5(1); reg 4(1) as amended |
| 2 | **Obtained first** — obtained *before* the worker performs the work that exceeds the limit ("unless his employer has first obtained...") | reg 4(1) as amended |
| 3 | **Made with the worker** — the worker's own agreement, not merely a management decision; a term in a contract of employment can serve, but it must be a genuine agreement, and the worker must not be subjected to detriment for refusing (see ERA 1996 ss.45A and 101A) | reg 5(1) |
| 4 | **Scope stated** — either a specified period or indefinite | reg 5(2)(a) |
| 5 | **Worker's right to terminate** — by written notice of not less than 7 days, unless the agreement provides a different notice period | reg 5(2)(b) |
| 6 | **Notice cap** — any notice period the agreement requires of the worker must not exceed 3 months | reg 5(3) |
| 7 | **Employer records** — up-to-date records identifying each worker who has agreed, setting out the terms of the agreement, and specifying hours worked in each reference period since the agreement took effect (excluding periods ended more than two years before the most recent entry) | reg 5(4)(a) |
| 8 | **Inspector access** — records produced to HSE/other reg 28 enforcing authority inspectors on request, with requested information about opted-out cases | reg 5(4)(b)-(c) |
| 9 | **Parallel duty** — the employer must keep up-to-date records of all workers carrying out work to which the limit does not apply because of the agreement | reg 4(2) as amended |

If any of 1-8 fails, the limit has not been excluded and the worker's average must be kept at or below 48.

### 2.2 What the opt-out does *not* do

- It removes **only** the reg 4(1) average. It does **not** displace the 8-hour average for night workers (reg 6), daily/weekly rest (regs 10-11), rest breaks (reg 12), annual leave (reg 13), or the reg 4(2) duty to take all reasonable steps to protect health and safety.
- It is **not available to young workers**, who have separate, more protective limits that cannot be opted out of.
- It does not convert the 48-hour figure into "no limit at all" as a matter of health and safety law: employers remain exposed under reg 4(2), H&S at Work etc. Act 1974, and the contract itself.

### 2.3 Secondary routes (flagged, so they are not confused with the answer to ask 2)

- **Varying the reference period** (reg 4(3) proviso, reg 4(5), reg 23(b) relevant agreement): stretches the measurement window; it does not lift the 48-hour rate.
- **Part III exceptions**, in particular the "unmeasured working time" exception (reg 20), which disapplies reg 4(1)-(2) where, on account of the specific characteristics of the work, the duration of working time is not measured or predetermined or can be determined by the worker themselves — the classic case being managing executives and similar autonomous roles. (Confirm current numbering against the consolidated text.)
- **Status**: someone who is not a "worker" within reg 2(1) (e.g. genuinely self-employed) is outside the Regulations altogether.

## 3. Drafting: a compliant opt-out clause

> **Agreement under regulation 5 of the Working Time Regulations 1998**
>
> 1. I, [name], agree with [employer] that the limit in regulation 4(1) of the Working Time Regulations 1998 (that my working time, including overtime, shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days in the applicable reference period) **shall not apply in my case**.
> 2. This agreement [applies indefinitely] / [relates to the period from [date] to [date]].
> 3. I may end this agreement at any time by giving written notice to [HR / named manager] of [not less than seven days]. *[If a longer period is used it must not exceed three months — reg 5(3).]*
> 4. I understand that entering into this agreement is voluntary, that I may decline or withdraw it, and that I will not be subjected to any detriment for declining or withdrawing.
> 5. I have had the opportunity to take advice on this agreement.
>
> Signed: ................................ (worker)   Date: ................
> For and on behalf of [employer]: ................................   Date: ................

**Opt-out register — minimum fields:** worker identifier; date agreement signed; whether time-limited or indefinite and its dates; notice terms; hours worked in each reference period since the agreement took effect (retain so that no period ending within two years of the most recent entry is lost); flag for inspector production.

## 4. Operational notes for the employer side

1. **Monitor the average, not the week.** Run the reg 4(6) calculation (A + B) / C per reference period; treat any result above 48 as a breach requiring action (reduce hours, extend the window by agreement, or rely on a valid opt-out).
2. **Pick the window deliberately.** Without a relevant agreement fixing successive 17-week periods, the worker/enforcer can test *any* 17-week window (reg 4(3)(b)) — a rolling check is the prudent control.
3. **Holiday/sick must not be scored as zero hours**; apply the excluded-days formula, or a returning worker will appear to breach.
4. **Withdrawal is a live risk.** The worker can terminate on 7 days' notice (or the agreed period, max 3 months); rosters must revert to <=48 average immediately on termination.
5. **Record-keeping is the enforcement hook.** Reg 5(4) records and inspector access are conditions of relying on the opt-out, not optional paperwork.

## 5. Currency and caveats

- The **48-hour figure and the reg 5 written-agreement mechanism** are stable across the as-made (1998) and current texts.
- Reg 4(1)-(2) were amended (the "unless his employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing" formulation and the express record-keeping duty in reg 4(2)); the amendments listed for reg 4 are 01/10/1998, 17/12/1999, 06/04/2003 and 01/01/2024. **Before relying on the detailed record-keeping wording of reg 5(4) in a live matter, check the consolidated text in force on the relevant date** — the text of reg 5 used here is the as-made version, and the record-keeping duties were revised with effect from 1 January 2024. The core requirements (written agreement, duration, 7-day worker notice, 3-month cap, records identifying opted-out workers and their terms, inspector access) are the operative ones.
- Northern Ireland: SR 1998/386, materially identical (enforcement via the Department). Great Britain: HSE and local authorities under reg 28.
- Not covered here because not asked: remedies and enforcement detail (reg 30 / EAT and tribunal routes), the night-work derogations, and sector-specific regimes (road transport, civil aviation, sea fishing, offshore).

RETENTION PERIODS UNDER 21 CFR § 211.180(a) — BATCH-ASSOCIATED RECORDS AND OTC PRODUCTS WITHOUT EXPIRATION DATING

=====================================================================
1. DIRECT ANSWER
=====================================================================

| # | Record class | Minimum retention period | Clock starts at |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Any production, control, or distribution record required by 21 CFR Part 211 that is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product | AT LEAST 1 YEAR | The expiration date of the batch |
| 2 | Same record class, but the batch is a "certain OTC drug product lacking expiration dating because [it] meet[s] the criteria for exemption under § 211.137" | 3 YEARS | The date the batch is distributed |

Both are MINIMUMS ("at least", "shall be retained"). A firm may retain longer; it may never retain for less.

Governing text: 21 CFR § 211.180(a), promulgated at 43 FR 45077 (Sept. 29, 1978), as amended at 60 FR 4091 (Jan. 20, 1995). Verified verbatim against three independent sources on 2026-11-17: eCFR (title 21, chapter I, subchapter C, part 211, subpart J), GovInfo CFR-2025-title21-vol4 (XML and PDF), and GovInfo CFR-2024-title21-vol4 (XML). All four renderings are word-for-word identical, so there is no version drift between the 2024 and 2025 annual editions on this paragraph.

=====================================================================
2. VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT (§ 211.180(a))
=====================================================================

"(a) Any production, control, or distribution record that is required to be maintained in compliance with this part and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch."

Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-211/subpart-J/section-211.180 (fetched 2026-11-17T05:42:43Z); corroborated by https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol4/xml/CFR-2025-title21-vol4-sec211-180.xml and the corresponding 2025 PDF.

=====================================================================
3. ELEMENT-BY-ELEMENT PARSE OF THE PROVISION
=====================================================================

The paragraph contains four operative elements. A record must satisfy (a) and (b) to fall inside it; (c) then selects which of the two clocks applies.

(a) SCOPE — "Any production, control, or distribution record ... required to be maintained in compliance with this part." The record must be one that Part 211 itself requires (e.g., batch production and control records under § 211.188, laboratory testing records under § 211.194, distribution records under § 211.196). Records kept only as a matter of company policy, and not required by Part 211, are outside this paragraph (firm policy or other law governs them).

(b) NEXUS — "... and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product." The record must be traceable to an identified batch. Records that are not batch-specific (e.g., master production and control records under § 211.186, general SOPs, validation reports, training files) are NOT governed by § 211.180(a); this paragraph supplies no period for them. See § 7 below — do not back-fill a number for those from this provision.

(c) DEFAULT CLOCK — "... shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch." The clock is anchored to the batch's expiration date, not to the manufacture date, the release date, or the distribution date. If the expiry is later extended by stability data, the anchor moves and the retention end-date must be recomputed; the required retention never shortens because a batch was shipped early.

(d) OTC EXEMPTION BRANCH — "... or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch." This branch applies only where BOTH conditions hold: (i) the product is an OTC drug product, and (ii) it lacks expiration dating specifically because it qualifies for the § 211.137 exemption. An OTC product that carries an expiration date falls under the 1-year-after-expiration rule, not this branch. Because there is no expiration date to anchor to, the regulation substitutes the distribution date and lengthens the period to 3 years.

Note on precision: the researched sources quote § 211.180(a) but do not quote § 211.137 itself. The specific paragraph letter of § 211.137 that houses the exemption criteria should therefore be confirmed against § 211.137 directly before it is written into an SOP; the citation "§ 211.137" as used in § 211.180(a) is exact and sufficient for this answer.

=====================================================================
4. DO NOT CONFUSE WITH § 211.180(b) (ADJACENT, DIFFERENT RULE)
=====================================================================

§ 211.180(b) covers a different record class — records for components, drug product containers, closures, and labeling — and uses a different anchor for its OTC branch:

"(b) Records shall be maintained for all components, drug product containers, closures, and labeling for at least 1 year after the expiration date or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under § 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the last lot of drug product incorporating the component or using the container, closure, or labeling."

Two distinctions that are frequently mis-stated in SOPs:
- (a) runs from the expiration date / distribution of THE BATCH; (b) runs from the expiration date / distribution of the LAST LOT that used the component, container, closure, or labeling. The (b) clock can therefore end later than any single batch's (a) clock.
- The numeric periods happen to be identical (1 year / 3 years), but they are separate obligations and must be tracked as separate record classes.

Also note § 211.170 (reserve samples) separately requires 3 years after distribution of the lot for an OTC product exempt from expiration dating under § 211.137. That is a physical-sample retention rule, not a records rule, and it is not the source of the 3 years in § 211.180(a) — the two provisions independently impose the same 3-year figure. (Sources also note § 211.170 was amended at 89 FR 51770, June 18, 2024, effective Dec. 18, 2025; that amendment does not alter § 211.180(a).)

=====================================================================
5. HOW TO APPLY IT — RETENTION END-DATE CALCULATION
=====================================================================

Rule 1 (dated batch):
  Retention_End_Date = Expiration_Date_of_Batch + 1 year
  Destroy no earlier than Retention_End_Date.

Rule 2 (OTC batch exempt from expiration dating under § 211.137):
  Retention_End_Date = Distribution_Date_of_Batch + 3 years
  Where a batch ships in multiple shipments, anchor to the LAST distribution date for that batch (the conservative and auditable reading, since the regulation says "after distribution of the batch").

Worked examples:
- Example A (dated Rx batch): expiration date 31 March 2027 → minimum retention through 31 March 2028.
- Example B (dated OTC batch with an expiration date): expiration date 30 September 2026 → minimum retention through 30 September 2027. The 3-year OTC branch does NOT apply, because the product bears expiration dating.
- Example C (OTC batch exempt from expiration dating under § 211.137): final shipment 15 June 2026 → minimum retention through 15 June 2029.
- Example D (expiry extension): batch originally expired 31 December 2026, extended by approved stability data to 31 December 2027 → retention end-date moves from 31 December 2027 to 31 December 2028.

Implementation controls:
- Store the anchor date and the applicable rule as explicit fields on the record (e.g., RETENTION_RULE = 'BATCH_EXPIRY_1Y' | 'OTC_NO_EXPIRY_3Y', ANCHOR_DATE, RETENTION_END_DATE). Do not compute retention from a free-text expiry field at destruction time.
- Prohibit destruction while any hold is open: litigation hold, FDA 483/inspection commitment, recall, or an open § 211.192 investigation touching the batch. § 211.180(a) sets a floor, not a ceiling; a hold extends it.
- Destruction must be blocked, not merely warned, when today's date < RETENTION_END_DATE.
- Keep the destruction record itself; it is the evidence that the floor was honored.

=====================================================================
6. RELATED § 211.180 OBLIGATIONS THAT AFFECT "HOW" BUT NOT "HOW LONG"
=====================================================================

- § 211.180(c): during the retention period, records (or copies) must be readily available for authorized inspection at the establishment where the activities occurred; records immediately retrievable from another location by computer or other electronic means satisfy this. So off-site or electronic archival is permitted, provided immediate retrieval is demonstrated.
- § 211.180(d): originals or true copies (photocopy, microfilm, microfiche, or other accurate reproduction) are acceptable; where reduction techniques are used, suitable reader and photocopying equipment must be readily available.
- § 211.180(e): written records must support at least annual evaluation of quality standards, including review of a representative number of batches and of complaints/recalls/returns/investigations. This is a use obligation; it does not shorten the retention floors above.
- § 211.180(f): notification procedures for investigations, recalls, inspectional observations, and GMP regulatory actions. Again procedural, not a retention period.

=====================================================================
7. SCOPE LIMITS — WHAT THIS ANSWER DOES NOT SAY
=====================================================================

- It does not set a retention period for records that are required by Part 211 but are NOT specifically associated with a batch (master production and control records under § 211.186, SOPs, validation and qualification records, training records, complaint files not tied to a batch). § 211.180(a) is silent on those; do not quote 1 year or 3 years for them from this provision. Confirm the applicable requirement separately (for example, § 211.180(e) annual product review inputs, § 211.198 complaint files, or firm policy).
- It does not address reserve samples (§ 211.170) or distribution-record content (§ 211.196); both are separate provisions.
- It does not address non-U.S. requirements. If a batch is also marketed in another jurisdiction, that jurisdiction may impose a different — sometimes longer — retention period, and the firm must apply the longest applicable requirement. Verify that regime separately; no non-U.S. figure is asserted here.
- It does not address records for products without a U.S. marketing application or for investigational drug product, which may be governed by other parts of Title 21.

=====================================================================
8. CITATIONS FOR VERIFICATION
=====================================================================

- 21 CFR § 211.180(a) and (b): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-211/subpart-J/section-211.180
- Annual edition (2025), XML: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol4/xml/CFR-2025-title21-vol4-sec211-180.xml
- Annual edition (2025), PDF: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol4/pdf/CFR-2025-title21-vol4-sec211-180.pdf
- Part 211 index (for § 211.137, § 211.170, § 211.188, § 211.194, § 211.196): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-211
- Source note for § 211.180: [43 FR 45077, Sept. 29, 1978, as amended at 60 FR 4091, Jan. 20, 1995]

=====================================================================
9. ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR CITATION IN AN SOP
=====================================================================

"Production, control, and distribution records specifically associated with a batch shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch or, for OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under 21 CFR § 211.137, for 3 years after distribution of the batch (21 CFR § 211.180(a))."
