MEMORANDUM — Rescission deadline under 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i)

1. ANSWER

(1) General rule. The consumer may exercise the right to rescind "until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last." The trigger is therefore the LAST of three events, not consummation alone, and the deadline is midnight at the end of the third business day counted from that last event.

(2) Never-delivered branch. "If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first." The outer limit is three years after consummation, cut short by a transfer of all of the consumer's interest or by a sale of the property.

2. GOVERNING TEXT (12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i), as currently published on eCFR and as confirmed unchanged in the 2021 printed CFR)

"(3)(i) The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act."

Two textual points that control the analysis and are frequently gotten wrong:

(a) The regulation contains no "one year after sale" rule. The expiration events are transfer of all of the consumer's interest, or sale of the property — full stop, with no grace period. Any workflow, checklist or system rule that encodes a one-year post-sale rescission tail under § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) is wrong and should be removed.

(b) The three-year figure is measured in years from consummation, not in business days, and it is not the same clock as the three-business-day window. The three-business-day window is the general rule; the three-year period is the consequence of non-delivery.

3. ASK 1 — HOW TO COMPUTE THE THREE-BUSINESS-DAY DEADLINE

3.1 Identify the three candidate events

- Consummation of the transaction (for open-end plans under § 1026.15, the occurrence giving rise to the right).
- Delivery of the notice required by § 1026.23(b): two copies to each consumer entitled to rescind (one copy each if delivered electronically in compliance with E-Sign), on a separate document identifying the transaction, disclosing the security interest, the right to rescind, how to exercise it with the form and the creditor's address, the effects of rescission, and the date the rescission period expires.
- Delivery of all material disclosures. Per § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii), "material disclosures" means the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g).

3.2 Take the latest of the three dates. The period does not begin to run until the last of them has occurred. Official interpretation ¶ 23(b)(1)-4 (Time of providing notice) states the notice need not be given before consummation, but "the rescission period will not begin to run until the notice is given": if the creditor provides the notice on May 15 but disclosures were given and the transaction consummated on May 10, the three-business-day period runs from May 15.

3.3 Count three business days forward from that date, excluding the trigger day itself. Use the rescission-specific business-day definition of § 1026.2(a)(6) (all calendar days except Sundays and the legal public holidays specified in 5 U.S.C. 6103(a)), not the "offices open" definition. That Saturdays count is confirmed arithmetically by the CFPB commentary examples: where consummation is Friday, June 1, and the disclosures and rescission notice were given Thursday, May 31, the period "will expire at midnight of the third business day after June 1 — that is, Tuesday, June 5" (Saturday June 2 = day 1, Monday June 4 = day 2, Tuesday June 5 = day 3); and where disclosures and consummation are Friday, June 1, with the rescission notice given Monday, June 4, the period expires "at midnight of the third business day after June 4 — that is, Thursday, June 7."

3.4 The deadline is midnight at the end of that third business day. Note that midnight is not further defined in the text quoted; where a transaction spans time zones, record the consumer's location and the creditor's receipt cut-off in the file rather than assuming.

3.5 Exercise is effective on dispatch, not receipt. Under § 1026.23(a)(2) the consumer notifies the creditor "by mail, telegram or other means of written communication," and notice "is considered given when mailed, when filed for telegraphic transmission or, if sent by other means, when delivered to the creditor's designated place of business." A notice mailed before midnight on the final day is timely even though it arrives later.

3.6 Multiple consumers. Section 1026.23(b)(1) requires delivery of the notice to each consumer entitled to rescind, and § 1026.23(a)(4) provides that "the exercise of the right by one consumer shall be effective as to all consumers." Practical consequence for a compliance system: compute the anchor date per consumer entitled to rescind (each consumer's own notice/material-disclosure delivery dates), and treat the earliest resulting deadline among them as the operative date on which the right can still be exercised by anyone, because one timely rescission voids the transaction for all.

4. ASK 2 — THE NEVER-DELIVERED BRANCH

4.1 If the § 1026.23(b) notice or the material disclosures are never delivered, the right does not lapse after three business days; it "shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer's interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first." Operationally: deadline = earliest of (i) the third anniversary of consummation, (ii) the date all of the consumer's interest in the property is transferred, (iii) the date the property is sold.

4.2 "Never delivered" means delivered neither at consummation nor at any later point. If the notice or material disclosures are delivered late — after consummation but before the three-year point — the three-business-day window restarts and runs from that later delivery (interpretation ¶ 23(b)(1)-4, quoted above). The three-year provision is written for the case where delivery does not happen at all; where delivery happens late, the operative measurement is three business days from the late delivery, and the three-year period functions as the outside limit (15 U.S.C. 1635(f); Jesinoski v. Countrywide Home Loans, Inc., 574 U.S. 259 (2015) — written notice within the period, not suit, effects rescission; the case authority is cited as background and is not part of the fetched regulation text).

4.3 One statutory extension is preserved inside the same sentence: "In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act." Flag any file involving a government-ordered or administrative rescission for that extension rather than applying the three-year figure mechanically.

5. THRESHOLD QUESTIONS THAT MUST BE ANSWERED BEFORE EITHER DATE IS COMPUTED

- Does the right exist at all? Section 1026.23(f) exempts residential mortgage transactions, refinancings/consolidations by the same creditor of credit already secured by the principal dwelling (except as to the excess amount financed), transactions in which a state agency is the creditor, certain subsequent advances in a series, and renewals of optional insurance premiums. No rescission deadline applies where there is no right.
- Was the right waived? Section 1026.23(e) permits a waiver in a personal financial emergency; a valid waiver ends the analysis.
- Is the three-business-day deadline measured against accurate disclosures? Sections 1026.23(g) (tolerances) and (h) (inaccurate or incomplete disclosures) bear on whether what was delivered counts as delivery of the material disclosures. The text of (g)–(h) was not part of the passages retrieved for this memorandum, so those provisions are identified as cross-references to be read in full before a file is closed as "disclosures delivered."
- Is the transaction open-end? Section 1026.15(a)(3) contains the parallel three-business-day / three-year structure for open-end plans, with the trigger being the occurrence that gives rise to the right. The analysis above maps onto it, but the citation for an open-end file should be § 1026.15, not § 1026.23.

6. DECISION PROCEDURE (implementable as written)

    rescissionDeadline(consummationDate, noticeDelivered, materialDisclosuresDelivered, transferAllInterestDate, saleDate, administrativeProceeding):
        if rightDoesNotApply under 23(f) or validWaiver under 23(e): return NO_RIGHT
        if noticeDelivered is NEVER or materialDisclosuresDelivered is NEVER:
            candidates = [ consummationDate + 3 years, transferAllInterestDate, saleDate ]   # ignore nulls
            deadline = earliest(candidates)
        else:
            anchor = max(consummationDate, latestNoticeDelivery, latestMaterialDisclosureDelivery)
            deadline = midnight at end of nthBusinessDay(after = anchor, n = 3)
                       # businessDay = Mon-Sat minus Sundays and 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) holidays
        if administrativeProceeding: apply 15 U.S.C. 1635(f) extension per sentence 3 of 23(a)(3)(i)
        return deadline

7. WORKED ILLUSTRATIONS (from the official interpretation)

- Consummation Friday, June 1; notice and material disclosures delivered Thursday, May 31 → anchor = June 1 → third business day = Tuesday, June 5 → deadline: midnight, Tuesday, June 5.
- Consummation and material disclosures Friday, June 1; notice delivered Monday, June 4 → anchor = June 4 → third business day = Thursday, June 7 → deadline: midnight, Thursday, June 7.
- Notice or material disclosures never delivered; consummation March 10, 2022; no transfer or sale → right expires March 10, 2025. If all of the consumer's interest is transferred, or the property is sold, on any earlier date, the right expires on that date instead.

8. CORRECTIONS TO THE PROJECT'S ASSUMPTION TABLE

- The assumption that a further expiration applies "not later than one year after sale or transfer of the interest" is not supported by § 1026.23(a)(3)(i) as published on eCFR or in the 2021 CFR volume. The regulation's expiration events on transfer/sale are immediate, not one year later. That assumption is dropped.
- The assumption that the question turns on the general rule rather than a dated fact pattern is adopted: the answers above are the rule as written, and any live file must supply the actual consummation, delivery, transfer and sale dates to produce a calendar date.
- "Business day" does matter to ask 1 (it is the unit of the three-day window and determines whether a Saturday counts) and does not matter to ask 2 (measured in years). Both are handled above.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 23 on consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/23 and 15 on consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/15. The first reads: "See interpretation of 23(b)(1) Notice of Right To Rescind in Supplement I"

question: P6
answer:
ANNUAL OCCUPATIONAL DOSE LIMITS FOR ADULT RADIATION WORKERS — 10 CFR § 20.1201(a)

Controlling source: 10 CFR § 20.1201, 'Occupational dose limits for adults,' paragraph (a). Verified against four authoritative renderings that agree verbatim: eCFR current (title 10, chapter I, part 20, subpart C, § 20.1201, fetched 2026-11-17), eCFR subpart C page, GPO CFR 2025 title 10 vol. 1 PDF (sec. 20-1201), and GPO CFR 2024 title 10 vol. 1 XML. Source note on the section: 56 FR 23396, May 21, 1991, as amended at 60 FR 20185 (Apr. 25, 1995); 63 FR 39482 (July 23, 1998); 67 FR 16304 (Apr. 5, 2002); 72 FR 68059 (Dec. 4, 2007). No amendment to paragraph (a) after Dec. 4, 2007 appears in any of the four renderings; the 91 FR 15772 (Mar. 30, 2026) amendment visible in Subpart F touches § 20.1501(d), not § 20.1201(a).

1. THE THREE REQUESTED LIMITS

| Quantity | Regulatory term (citation) | Limit (rems) | Limit (sieverts) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total effective dose equivalent | TEDE — § 20.1201(a)(1)(i) | 5 rem | 0.05 Sv |
| Lens of the eye | Lens dose equivalent — § 20.1201(a)(2)(i) | 15 rem | 0.15 Sv |
| Skin of the whole body | Shallow-dose equivalent — § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii) | 50 rem | 0.5 Sv |

Regulation text, quoted exactly:

§ 20.1201(a): 'The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.'

§ 20.1201(a)(1): 'An annual limit, which is the more limiting of — (i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or (ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).'

§ 20.1201(a)(2): 'The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are: (i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and (ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity.'

2. UNIT CONVENTION
All conversions use the exact conventional relation 1 rem = 0.01 Sv (1 Sv = 100 rem), which is the convention the regulation itself uses parenthetically: 5 rems (0.05 Sv); 15 rems (0.15 Sv); 50 rem (0.5 Sv). Arithmetic check: 5 x 0.01 = 0.05; 15 x 0.01 = 0.15; 50 x 0.01 = 0.50. No rounding is involved; each Sv figure is exact under that convention.

3. HOW EACH LIMIT IS INTERPRETED AND APPLIED (necessary to use the numbers correctly)
- TEDE, 5 rem/yr: the total effective dose equivalent, i.e., the sum of the deep-dose equivalent from external exposure and the committed effective dose equivalent from intakes of radioactive material (§ 20.1003 definitions; summation rules in § 20.1202). It is the primary whole-body limit.
- Lens of the eye, 15 rem/yr: a lens dose equivalent, assessed at the lens depth (typically Hp(0.3)). It is a separate limit and is expressly excluded from the TEDE/organ summation (§ 20.1202 note: 'The dose equivalents for the lens of the eye, the skin, and the extremities are not included in the summation, but are subject to separate limits').
- Skin of the whole body, 50 rem/yr: a shallow-dose equivalent (typically Hp(0.07)), and per § 20.1201(c) it 'must be the dose averaged over the contiguous 10 square centimeters of skin receiving the highest exposure' — i.e., a 50 rem limit on a 1 cm²-averaged-at-10-cm² basis, not a uniform whole-body surface average.
- The three limits are concurrent, not additive: a worker may be at the TEDE limit while the lens and skin are separately governed by their own numbers.

4. TWO 50-rem FIGURES — DO NOT CONFLATE
The number 50 rem appears twice in § 20.1201(a) with different meanings:
- § 20.1201(a)(1)(ii): 50 rems (0.5 Sv) = deep-dose equivalent PLUS committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue OTHER THAN THE LENS, as the alternative branch of the 'more limiting of' test in (a)(1). This is NOT the TEDE limit and is outside the three items requested.
- § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii): 50 rem (0.5 Sv) = shallow-dose equivalent to the SKIN of the whole body or of any extremity. This is the requested skin limit.
The TEDE limit is 5 rem, never 50 rem.

5. SCOPE BOUNDARIES (stated so the three numbers are not misapplied)
In scope and answered: the three limits named in the request.
Deliberately not answered, because the request names only TEDE, lens, and whole-body skin: the organ/tissue branch of (a)(1)(ii); the skin-of-extremities limit (same 50 rem value as skin of whole body, but a distinct quantity); planned special exposure allowances (§ 20.1206: 5 x annual limit in a lifetime, and the (e)(1)/(e)(2) subtraction rules); minors at 10% of adult limits (§ 20.1207); the declared-pregnant-worker limit of 0.5 rem to the embryo/fetus (§ 20.1208); and the public dose limit (§ 20.1301).
Note for practice, not part of the numeric answer: these are limits, not goals — § 20.1101 requires ALARA below them; § 20.1502 triggers individual monitoring at 10% of the § 20.1201(a) limits; § 20.1201(f) requires reducing the current-year allowance by occupational dose received while employed by any other person; § 20.1201(b) requires subtracting doses in excess of the annual limits from planned-special-exposure allowances.

6. VERSION / AS-OF STATEMENT
The figures above are the current text of 10 CFR § 20.1201(a) as of the 2026-11-17 fetch, and are identical in the 2024 and 2025 GPO CFR editions. No state-agreement or historical variant is represented. If a specific as-of date or a state-analog rule (e.g., an Agreement State adoption with a different lens limit) governs the reader's program, that must be checked against that jurisdiction's rule; the federal figures are as stated here.

question: P8
answer:
# Fall Protection Trigger and Required Systems — 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1)

## 1. Direct answer

| Item | Answer |
|---|---|
| Trigger height (Ask 1) | **6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level** |
| Required protection (Ask 2) | **Guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems** (employer may choose any one or more of the three) |

## 2. Controlling regulatory text (verbatim)

**29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1) — Unprotected sides and edges:**

> "Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems."

Source verified against: eCFR 29 CFR 1926.501 (current); GovInfo CFR 2025 Title 29 Vol. 8 § 1926.501; CFR 2024 and CFR 2023 XML editions of the same section. The operative sentence is textually identical in all editions checked (2023, 2024, 2025), i.e., the 6-ft trigger is stable current law.

## 3. How the trigger is applied (procedure)

1. **Identify the walking/working surface.** The parenthetical in the standard is explicit: horizontal *and vertical* surfaces both count. Formwork faces, structural members used as walkways, and similar vertical surfaces are within (b)(1) unless a more specific paragraph of (b) applies.
2. **Identify the unprotected side or edge.** An edge is unprotected if there is no guardrail system, safety net system, personal fall arrest system, cover, or other § 1926.502-compliant barrier between the employee and the drop. A perimeter with a compliant guardrail is not an "unprotected" edge.
3. **Measure to the lower level.** Measure vertically from the walking/working surface on which the employee stands to the surface the employee would strike — the *lowest* level to which the employee is exposed at that edge, not merely the level immediately below. Where an employee is exposed to more than one lower level from the same edge, the lowest governs. The metric equivalent in the standard is 1.8 m.
4. **Apply the threshold.** At **6 ft (1.8 m) or more**, protection is mandatory. Below 6 ft, (b)(1) does not require it (other paragraphs of § 1926.501 may still apply — see § 5).
5. **Select and install a system** from the three named in (b)(1), built to the criteria in § 1926.502 (see § 4).
6. **Document** the measurement, the selected system, and the installation/inspection records.

## 4. The three permitted systems and their governing criteria

The statute permits **any** of the three; it does not rank them or require a specific one. Each must satisfy its criteria in § 1926.502:

| System | Criteria paragraph | Representative design requirements |
|---|---|---|
| Guardrail system | § 1926.502(b) | Top edge height of top rail 42 in ± 3 in above the walking/working surface; midrail, screening, or equivalent protection between top rail and surface; capable of withstanding a 200-lb force applied in any outward or downward direction at any point along the top edge |
| Safety net system | § 1926.502(c) | Installed as close as practicable below the working surface and in no case more than 30 ft (9.1 m) below it; drop-tested or certified; unobstructed fall path into the net; inspected weekly and after any impact |
| Personal fall arrest system | § 1926.502(d) | Full-body harness; anchorage capable of supporting 5,000 lb per employee attached, or designed/installed under supervision of a qualified person as part of a complete system with a safety factor of at least 2; maximum deceleration distance 3.5 ft (1.1 m); no free fall in excess of 6 ft; prompt rescue capability |

*Note on citation precision:* the § 1926.502 paragraph letters above (b)/(c)/(d) are certain; the subparagraph numbers for the 42-in rail, 5,000-lb anchorage, 3.5-ft deceleration, and 30-ft net placement should be re-verified against the current § 1926.502 text before being quoted in an enforcement or citation document.

## 5. What (b)(1) does NOT provide — and what changes the answer

- **No infeasibility exception.** § 1926.501(b)(1) has no exception for infeasible or greater-hazard conditions, and it does not authorize substitution of a § 1926.502(k) fall protection plan. That alternative exists in the standard only where a paragraph grants it — e.g., **leading edges under § 1926.501(b)(2)(i)** — and there the employer bears the burden of establishing infeasibility, with a presumption that at least one listed system is feasible and will not create a greater hazard. **Do not apply the (k) plan option to a plain (b)(1) unprotected side or edge.**
- **More specific paragraphs of (b) displace (b)(1).** Where the exposure fits a specific paragraph, that paragraph's requirements govern; (b)(15) is the residual catch-all and applies only to walking/working surfaces not addressed by (b)(1) through (b)(14). Relevant quoted examples, all keyed to the same 6-ft (1.8 m) trigger but with differing permitted systems:
  - **(b)(2)(i) Leading edges** — 6 ft or more: guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest; infeasibility exception with a § 1926.502(k) plan.
  - **(b)(8) Dangerous equipment** — under 6 ft: guardrail systems or equipment guards; 6 ft or more: guardrail, personal fall arrest, or safety net.
  - **(b)(9) Overhand bricklaying** — 6 ft or more: guardrail, safety net, personal fall arrest, **or a controlled access zone**.
  - **(b)(14) Wall openings** — outside bottom edge 6 ft or more above lower levels and inside bottom edge less than 39 in (1.0 m) above the walking/working surface: guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest.
  - **(b)(15) Walking/working surfaces not otherwise addressed** — 6 ft or more: guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest.
- **Scope exclusions.** § 1926.501(b)(15) expressly excepts workplaces covered by § 1926.500(a)(2). Confirm the activity is within Subpart M's scope before applying (b)(1).
- **Other thresholds in other subparts are separate and higher, and are NOT (b)(1).** Scaffold work under Subpart L and steel erection under Subpart R carry their own trigger heights (10 ft and 15 ft respectively). Those are different rules for different scopes; they neither raise nor lower the 6-ft (1.8 m) trigger of § 1926.501(b)(1). Do not blend them.

## 6. Verification checklist (for a competent engineer applying this)

- [ ] Edge identified and confirmed unprotected (no compliant guardrail, net, PFAS, or cover).
- [ ] Vertical distance measured from the working surface to the **lowest** exposed lower level.
- [ ] Distance recorded as ≥ 6 ft (1.8 m) or < 6 ft (1.8 m).
- [ ] If ≥ 6 ft: system chosen from the three in (b)(1) and verified against § 1926.502(b)/(c)/(d).
- [ ] Confirmed that no more specific paragraph of § 1926.501(b) governs (leading edge, dangerous equipment, overhand bricklaying, wall opening, etc.).
- [ ] Confirmed no § 1926.500(a)(2) scope exclusion applies.
- [ ] If a fall protection plan is being used, confirmed the governing paragraph actually authorizes it (it is not authorized by (b)(1) alone).

## 7. Bottom line

Under 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1), an employee on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is **6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level** must be protected from falling by **a guardrail system, a safety net system, or a personal fall arrest system** — the employer's choice among the three, each built to § 1926.502 criteria.

question: P10
answer:
SCOPE AND STATUS
This is a legal summary, not legal advice. It addresses the Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833) as they apply in England and Wales and Scotland (the regulations are marked E+W+S). Northern Ireland has parallel working time regulations and is outside this note. The note is based on the text of reg 4 and reg 5 as made and subsequently amended; before relying on it, check the latest revised version on legislation.gov.uk for any amendments after the version consulted.

1. THE LIMIT: 48 HOURS AVERAGE PER SEVEN DAYS, OVERTIME INCLUDED
Regulation 4(1) provides that, unless the employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work (the original wording was 'Subject to regulation 5'), a worker's working time, including overtime, in any reference period applicable in the worker's case shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days.

Key points:
- The figure is 48 hours. It is an average over the reference period, not a hard cap of 48 hours in every single week. A worker may work more than 48 hours in a particular week provided the average over the applicable reference period does not exceed 48 hours per seven days.
- The ordinary reference period is 17 weeks (reg 4(3)). If the worker has worked for the employer for less than 17 weeks, the reference period is the period since the worker started (reg 4(4)).
- For a worker excluded from the scope of certain provisions by regulation 21, the 17-week references are replaced by 26 weeks (reg 4(5)).
- A relevant agreement under regulation 23(b) may modify the reference period; reg 4(3) is expressly subject to such an agreement.
- The average is calculated under reg 4(6) using the formula (A + B) / C, where A is the aggregate hours of working time in the reference period, B is the aggregate hours in the subsequent period ending when the number of days worked equals the number of excluded days, and C is the number of weeks in the reference period. Excluded days under reg 4(7) include annual leave under reg 13, sick leave, maternity leave (and, as amended, paternity, adoption or parental leave), and periods in respect of which the reg 4(1) limit did not apply because of a reg 5 opt-out agreement.
- The employer must take all reasonable steps, in keeping with the need to protect health and safety, to ensure that the reg 4(1) limit is complied with for each worker to whom it applies (reg 4(2)).

2. HOW A WORKER IS TAKEN OUTSIDE THE LIMIT: THE REGULATION 5 WRITTEN AGREEMENT
Regulation 5(1) provides that the reg 4(1) limit shall not apply in relation to a worker who has agreed with the employer in writing that it should not apply in the worker's case, provided the employer complies with reg 5(4). This is commonly called the individual opt-out.

The operative steps are:
(a) The employer must first obtain the worker's agreement in writing. The current reg 4(1) wording requires the employer to have 'first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work'. An implied, informal or purely collective agreement is not sufficient for reg 5; the individual worker must have agreed in writing.
(b) The agreement may relate to a specified period or apply indefinitely (reg 5(2)(a)).
(c) The worker may terminate the agreement by giving not less than seven days' notice in writing to the employer, subject to any provision in the agreement for a different period of notice (reg 5(2)(b)). Where the agreement provides for termination after a period of notice, that notice period must not exceed three months (reg 5(3)).
(d) The employer must comply with the record-keeping requirements in reg 5(4). The employer must maintain up-to-date records which: identify each worker who has agreed that the reg 4(1) limit should not apply; set out the terms on which the worker so agreed; and specify the number of hours worked by that worker for the employer during each reference period since the agreement came into effect, excluding any period which ended more than two years before the most recent entry in the records. The employer must permit any inspector appointed by the Health and Safety Executive or any other authority responsible under reg 28 for enforcement to inspect those records on request, and must provide such an inspector with such information as may be requested regarding any case in which a worker has agreed that the limit should not apply.
(e) If the employer does not comply with reg 5(4), the reg 5(1) exclusion is not made out. The opt-out must be genuine and voluntary; an employer should not treat a worker's refusal to agree as a breach of contract or as a ground for detriment.

Effect: while a valid reg 5 agreement is in force, the reg 4(1) average limit does not apply to that worker. The opt-out does not remove the separate night-work limits, rest entitlements, annual leave rights, or the employer's general health and safety duties. Special limits apply to young workers (under 18), and those are outside this note.

3. OTHER ROUTES OUTSIDE REG 4(1) (NOT INDIVIDUAL OPT-OUTS)
- Regulation 21 contains category-based exclusions from certain provisions, for example workers whose working time is not measured or predetermined or can be determined by the worker themselves, and certain other categories specified in reg 21. Those workers are outside the relevant provisions by status, not by a reg 5 agreement.
- A relevant agreement under reg 23(b) may modify the reference period, but it does not remove the 48-hour average limit.
- Sector-specific derogations in Part III of the Regulations may apply to particular categories of worker; those are separate from the reg 5 individual opt-out.

In short: the limit is an average of 48 hours per seven days, overtime included, over the applicable reference period (ordinarily 17 weeks); the individual route by which a worker is taken outside reg 4(1) is a prior written agreement with the employer under reg 5, supported by the reg 5(4) records, terminable by the worker on at least seven days' written notice (subject to any different notice period, which cannot exceed three months).

question: P12
answer:
RETENTION OF BATCH-ASSOCIATED RECORDS UNDER 21 CFR 211.180(a)

=== BOTTOM LINE ===

| Record set | Minimum retention | Clock starts |
|---|---|---|
| Production, control, or distribution records required by Part 211 and specifically associated with a batch of a drug product (the general rule) | 1 year | On the batch's expiration date |
| Same records for a "certain OTC drug product" that lacks expiration dating because it meets the exemption criteria of 21 CFR 211.137 | 3 years | On distribution of the batch |

Both are floors ("at least"), not ceilings, and the two rules are alternatives — you apply one or the other to a given batch, never both added together.

=== CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim) ===

21 CFR 211.180(a):

"(a) Any production, control, or distribution record that is required to be maintained in compliance with this part and is specifically associated with a batch of a drug product shall be retained for at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch or, in the case of certain OTC drug products lacking expiration dating because they meet the criteria for exemption under Sec. 211.137, 3 years after distribution of the batch."

Source history line: "[43 FR 45077, Sept. 29, 1978, as amended at 60 FR 4091, Jan. 20, 1995]". The paragraph has not been amended since 1995.

Currency check performed: identical wording confirmed in (i) eCFR current Title 21, Part 211, Subpart J; (ii) the 2025 print CFR, Title 21, Volume 4 (revision date 2025-04-01), both PDF and XML; (iii) a second eCFR URL for the same section; and (iv) the govinfo PDF of Sec. 211.170, which reproduces Sec. 211.180 in the running text. The 2024 amendment at 89 FR 51770 (June 18, 2024), effective December 18, 2025, touches Sec. 211.170 (reserve samples), not Sec. 211.180(a), so it does not change either answer.

=== ASK 1 — GENERAL BATCH RECORD RETENTION ===

Answer: at least 1 year after the expiration date of the batch.

Elements that must all be satisfied for the rule to attach:
1. The record is a production, control, or distribution record.
2. It is "required to be maintained in compliance with this part" — i.e., it is a Part 211 record (batch production and control records under 211.188, laboratory determination records under 211.194, distribution records under 211.196, reconciliation/inventory records under 211.184, etc.).
3. It is "specifically associated with a batch" — it ties to an identifiable lot/batch.

Start date: the expiration date assigned to that batch (the date on the batch's label/expiry assignment), not the manufacture date and not the release date.

Worked date arithmetic:
- Batch expiration date 30 June 2027 -> retain through at least 30 June 2028; destruction on or after 1 July 2028.
- Batch expiration date 31 December 2026 -> retain through at least 31 December 2027.

Practical note on the clock: a batch with a 24-month expiry manufactured in January 2026 has an expiry in January 2028 and a Federal floor running to January 2029 — roughly three years from manufacture. The "1 year" figure is measured from expiry, not from manufacture, so do not schedule destruction off the batch record date.

=== ASK 2 — OTC PRODUCTS LACKING EXPIRATION DATING ===

Answer: 3 years after distribution of the batch.

Elements of the carve-out:
1. The product is an OTC drug product.
2. It lacks expiration dating.
3. It lacks expiration dating *because* it meets the criteria for exemption under 21 CFR 211.137. The exemption must be a genuine 211.137 exemption, documented in the firm's records; a product that simply has no assigned expiry for other reasons does not qualify for this branch and is instead a compliance gap (a non-exempt product with no expiry date cannot borrow the 3-year figure to cure the omission).

Start date: distribution of the batch. Where a batch ships in multiple lots over a period, the conservative and defensible practice is to run the clock from the last distribution date for that batch, which guarantees the full 3 years from every shipment. Document the distribution date(s) relied on.

Worked date arithmetic:
- Last distribution of batch 15 March 2026 -> retain through at least 15 March 2029.
- Last distribution of batch 2 November 2025 -> retain through at least 2 November 2028.

Interaction with the general rule: the two branches are disjunctive in the regulation ("or, in the case of..."). For a 211.137-exempt OTC product with no expiry date, the 3-year post-distribution period is the only applicable clock. If a firm voluntarily assigns an expiration date to such a product, the general branch (1 year after that expiration date) is the literal fit; as a conservative control, apply whichever period expires later and record the basis chosen.

=== ADJACENT PROVISIONS — DO NOT SUBSTITUTE THESE NUMBERS ===

- 21 CFR 211.180(b) — components, drug product containers, closures, and labeling: at least 1 year after the expiration date, or, for 211.137-exempt OTC products lacking expiration dating, 3 years after distribution of the **last lot of drug product incorporating the component or using the container, closure, or labeling**. This is a different record set and a different trigger (last using lot) than 211.180(a)'s "distribution of the batch." Do not apply the (b) trigger to batch-specific records or vice versa.
- 21 CFR 211.170(b)(3) — reserve samples for an OTC drug product exempt from bearing an expiration date under 211.137: 3 years after the lot or batch is distributed. Same 3-year figure, but this governs physical reserve samples, not paper/electronic records; retaining records does not discharge the sample obligation, and vice versa.
- 21 CFR 211.180(e) — annual product quality review: requires written records to be maintained so data can be used for at least annual evaluation; this does not shorten either period.

=== FLOORS, NOT TARGETS: WHEN YOU MUST RETAIN LONGER ===

"At least" means the Federal minimum can be exceeded by other obligations. Retain beyond the 211.180(a) period, and place the batch records on hold, when any of the following attaches:
- An investigation under 211.192 (discrepancy, failure, out-of-specification) is open or referenced by the batch record.
- A complaint, returned/salvaged product review, or recall affects the batch — recall records and distribution records needed to trace a recall must remain available for the duration of the recall action.
- Stability data or commitment protocols designate the batch as a supporting/registration batch (retain for the life of the commitment, typically the marketed life of the product plus the post-expiry window).
- Litigation hold, subpoena, or FDA 704(a) inspection request (records requested during an inspection must be produced and must not be destroyed while the matter is open).
- Any State, territorial, or non-US requirement applicable to the establishment or market — outside the scope of this answer; see Scope Limits.

=== STORAGE AND AVAILABILITY CONDITIONS THAT TRAVEL WITH THE PERIOD ===

- 211.180(c): records, or copies, must be readily available for authorized inspection **during the retention period** at the establishment where the recorded activities occurred; records immediately retrievable from another location by computer or other electronic means satisfy this.
- 211.180(d): originals or true copies (photocopies, microfilm, microfiche, or other accurate reproductions) are acceptable; if reduction techniques such as microfilming are used, suitable reader and photocopying equipment must be readily available.
- Implication for electronic systems: an archival/e-signature system is acceptable only if the record remains retrievable and readable for the full period and the retrieval is immediate; a backup that requires a restore request may fail 211.180(c).

=== DECISION PROCEDURE FOR THE RECORD HOLDER ===

1. Classify the record: is it a production, control, or distribution record required by Part 211 and specifically tied to one batch? If no, 211.180(a) is not the controlling provision — check 211.180(b) or the specific section.
2. Ask whether the batch is an OTC drug product lacking expiration dating by reason of a documented 211.137 exemption.
   - Yes -> retention end = last distribution date of the batch + 3 years.
   - No -> retention end = labeled expiration date of the batch + 1 year.
3. Record the computed earliest destruction date on the record (or in the records-retention system) at the time of batch disposition, together with the trigger date used and its source document (expiry assignment or distribution record).
4. Apply any hold from the longer-retention list above; the later date governs.
5. At the computed date, verify no hold is open, then destroy and log the destruction (record identity, batch, date, method, approver).

=== SCOPE LIMITS AND CAVEATS ===

- Jurisdiction: US Federal (21 CFR Part 211) only. State retention requirements (e.g., State boards of pharmacy, State drug pedigree/record laws) and non-US requirements (EU GMP Chapter 4 / Annex 11, and similar) are not analyzed here and may be longer.
- Role: the obligation under 211.180(a) falls on the establishment that holds the records required by Part 211; a distributor that is not the manufacturer should confirm separately which records it is itself required to maintain (e.g., 211.196 distribution records) and for how long.
- 21 CFR 211.137's specific exemption criteria are referenced but not restated here; they were not retrieved in this pass and should be read from the current text before relying on the OTC branch. If a product's exempt status is undocumented, treat it as non-exempt and apply the general rule.
- This is a regulatory-text analysis, not legal advice for a specific enforcement matter.

# NIST SP 800-63B-4 — Password Length Requirements (Verifier Side)

## 1. Answers

| # | Question | Answer | Normative verb |
|---|----------|--------|----------------|
| 1 | Minimum length verifiers must require for a password used as a **single-factor** authentication mechanism | **15 characters** | SHALL (mandatory) |
| 2 | Minimum length for a password used **only as part of multi-factor** authentication | **8 characters** | SHALL (mandatory floor); verifiers MAY allow shorter than 15 but SHALL NOT go below 8 |
| 3 | Maximum length verifiers should **permit at least** | **64 characters** | SHOULD (recommended; a floor on the cap, not a ceiling on the password) |

**Citation:** NIST SP 800-63B-4, *Digital Identity Guidelines — Authentication and Authenticator Management*, Sec. **3.1.1.2 “Password Verifiers”** (Password requirements list, items 1 and 2). Confirmed identical in both renderings of the final revision:
- HTML: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/ (and https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html)
- PDF: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-63b-4.2pd.pdf

## 2. Verbatim source text (the only passage needed to verify all three values)

> “Verifiers and CSPs **SHALL** require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of **15 characters** in length. Verifiers and CSPs **MAY** allow passwords that are only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes to be shorter but **SHALL** require them to be a minimum of **eight characters** in length.
>
> Verifiers and CSPs **SHOULD** permit a maximum password length of at least **64 characters**.
>
> Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD accept all printing ASCII [RFC20] characters and the space character in passwords.
>
> Verifiers and CSPs SHOULD accept Unicode [ISO/ISC 10646] characters in passwords. **Each Unicode code point SHALL be counted as a single character when evaluating password length.**
>
> Verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT impose other composition rules (e.g., requiring mixtures of different character types) for passwords.
>
> Verifiers and CSPs SHALL NOT require subscribers to change passwords periodically. However, verifiers SHALL force a change if there is evidence that the authenticator has been compromised.”

Supporting usability text (same section family, §8/§3.1.1 usability guidance): “Allow at least 64 characters in length to support the use of passphrases.” — consistent with the 64-character cap floor.

## 3. How the three requirements interlock (read this before implementing)

- The 15-character rule is scoped to **single-factor** use: a password that by itself can complete an authentication event. If a login can succeed with the password alone, that credential is single-factor and 15 is the mandatory minimum — the fact that MFA is *available* on the account does not lower it.
- The 8-character rule is scoped to passwords “**only** used as part of multi-factor authentication processes” — i.e., the authentication event cannot complete without a second factor. This is a **floor, not a target**: 8 is the least a verifier may accept, and the verifier retains discretion to require up to 15 (or more) in that context.
- The 64-character rule is a **floor on the maximum**: a verifier must not reject a password merely for being long at 64 characters. It is not a maximum length of 64; passwords longer than 64 SHOULD continue to be accepted. Truncating input at 64 characters is non-conforming (and silently breaks long passphrases).
- Counting unit is the **Unicode code point**, not bytes and not grapheme clusters. A 15-code-point password may be far more than 15 bytes in UTF-8; a length check done on `bytes` is non-conforming and would reject valid non-ASCII passwords.
- No composition rules (no “must contain a digit/symbol/mixed case”), no periodic rotation, no hints. These sit in the same requirement block and are commonly implemented alongside the length checks.

## 4. Revision trap — do not answer from a draft

The values above are from the **final** SP 800-63B-4. Earlier text differs and is a frequent source of wrong answers:

| Document | Single-factor minimum | MFA-only minimum | Cap floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| SP 800-63B-3 (2017) | 8 (SHALL) | 8 (no distinction) | 64 (SHOULD) |
| SP 800-63B-4 **ipd** (2024 draft) | 8 (SHALL) | 8 (no distinction) | 64 (SHOULD) |
| SP 800-63B-4 **2pd** (Aug 2024 draft) | 8 (SHALL) + 15 (SHOULD) | 8 | 64 (SHOULD) |
| **SP 800-63B-4 final** | **15 (SHALL)** | **8 (SHALL)** | **64 (SHOULD)** |

If a source says “SHALL require a minimum of eight characters and SHOULD require a minimum of 15,” that is the 2pd draft, not the final. The final made 15 mandatory for single-factor and introduced the explicit MFA-only 8-character floor.

**Do not confuse the 8 here with other memorized-secret categories in the same publication:**
- *Activation secrets* (Sec. 3.2.10): SHALL be at least **4** characters, SHOULD be at least **6** — these are local unlock secrets inside a multi-factor authenticator, not verifier-facing passwords.
- *Look-up secrets* (Sec. 3.1.2): at least **6** decimal digits.
- *CSP/verifier-generated random passwords*: at least **6** characters (not subscriber-chosen).

## 5. Enforcement specification (backend implementation)

### 5.1 Constants

```python
# password_policy.py — NIST SP 800-63B-4, Sec. 3.1.1.2

MIN_LEN_SINGLE_FACTOR = 15   # SHALL — password can authenticate alone
MIN_LEN_MFA_ONLY      = 8    # SHALL floor — password only ever used with a 2nd factor
MAX_LEN_FLOOR         = 64   # SHOULD — must ACCEPT at least this many characters

# Hard upper bound is an engineering choice (DoS/abuse), not a NIST number.
# If you set one, it must be >= MAX_LEN_FLOOR and you must not reject on length
# below it. 1024 code points is a common non-restrictive choice.
MAX_LEN_HARD = 1024


def min_length_for(auth_policy: str) -> int:
    """auth_policy: 'single_factor' | 'mfa_only' — the account's configured
    authentication policy, NOT a property of the input field."""
    if auth_policy == 'single_factor':
        return MIN_LEN_SINGLE_FACTOR
    if auth_policy == 'mfa_only':
        return MIN_LEN_MFA_ONLY
    raise ValueError(f'unknown auth policy: {auth_policy!r}')


def password_length(pw: str) -> int:
    # Python str length == number of Unicode code points, which is what
    # SP 800-63B-4 requires ('each Unicode code point SHALL be counted as a
    # single character'). Do NOT use len(pw.encode('utf-8')) and do NOT
    # normalize/collapse before counting.
    return len(pw)


def validate_password(pw: str, auth_policy: str) -> None:
    n = password_length(pw)
    lo = min_length_for(auth_policy)
    if n < lo:
        raise PolicyError(
            code='password_too_short',
            message=f'Password must be at least {lo} characters.',
            required_min=lo, actual=n,
        )
    if n > MAX_LEN_HARD:
        raise PolicyError(
            code='password_too_long',
            message=f'Password must be at most {MAX_LEN_HARD} characters.',
            required_max=MAX_LEN_HARD, actual=n,
        )
    # No composition rules (SHALL NOT). No periodic expiry (SHALL NOT).
    # Blocklist comparison (common/breached/context words) belongs here too —
    # it is a separate SHALL in the same section, not a length rule.
```

### 5.2 Where to enforce

1. **Write path (enrollment / password change):** reject below the minimum for the account's target authentication policy, before hashing. Rejecting after hashing wastes an Argon2id/bcrypt run.
2. **Read path (login) — legacy credentials:** if a stored password predates the current policy (e.g., an 8-character password on an account now configured single-factor), the length rule cannot be retroactively satisfied by the verifier. The publication states the requirement without an explicit grandfather clause; the conforming operational pattern is to enforce at next change and force a reset for credentials below the applicable minimum, rather than to reject the login outright (which would lock out the subscriber). Record this as an explicit, documented exception with a remediation deadline — it is an engineering decision, not quoted NIST text.
3. **Policy resolution must be server-side.** Never let the client tell you which minimum applies. The `auth_policy` value comes from the account/AAL configuration stored in the database, not from the request body.
4. **MFA downgrade hazard:** if an account can fall back to password-only login (e.g., “remember this device,” or an IdP that silently skips the second factor), its password is single-factor and must meet 15. Audit any fallback path before allowing the 8-character floor for that account.

### 5.3 Test vectors (use these as unit tests)

| auth_policy | input length (code points) | expected |
|---|---|---|
| single_factor | 14 | reject (`password_too_short`, required_min=15) |
| single_factor | 15 | accept |
| single_factor | 64 | accept |
| single_factor | 200 | accept |
| mfa_only | 7 | reject (`password_too_short`, required_min=8) |
| mfa_only | 8 | accept |
| mfa_only | 14 | accept (shorter than 15 is permitted here) |
| mfa_only | 64 | accept |
| single_factor | 15 non-ASCII code points (e.g. 15 × 'é' or 15 × '🔐') | accept — counted as 15 characters |
| single_factor | 15 code points encoded in >15 UTF-8 bytes | accept — byte length must not be used |
| any | 1025 (if MAX_LEN_HARD=1024) | reject (`password_too_long`) |

## 6. Verification procedure (for a reviewer checking this answer against the source)

1. Open https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/ and locate Sec. **3.1.1.2 Password Verifiers**.
2. Search the page for the string `single-factor authentication mechanism` — the sentence ending `minimum of 15 characters in length` confirms answer 1.
3. In the same sentence, `only used as part of multi-factor authentication processes ... minimum of eight characters in length` confirms answer 2.
4. The next sentence, `permit a maximum password length of at least 64 characters`, confirms answer 3.
5. Confirm the page is the **final** -4 (URL path `800-63-4`, not `800-63-3`, and not a `-4.ipd`/`-4.2pd` draft filename). If step 2's 15-character single-factor sentence is absent, you are on a draft and the table in §4 applies.

All three values come from a single, contiguous, quoted passage; no derivation or inference is involved.

The first reads: "All printing ASCII [RFC20] characters as well as the space character SHOULD be acceptable in memorized secrets."
